title: Do Southeast Asian Employees Fear AI? It Depends Who's Asking.
summary: Three AI surveys of Southeast Asian workers, three different answers. Why the data conflicts, and why your own people are the only reliable source.
body_markdown:
If you're planning an AI rollout in Southeast Asia, you've probably seen a headline telling you how employees feel about it. You've probably also seen another one saying the exact opposite.


Both are based on real surveys. Both are worth reading. And neither tells you what your own employees think.


## Three surveys, three different answers


Here's what this year's major studies found:


Study


Who was asked


Headline finding


Milieu Insight


3,000 workers across Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam


53% rank over-dependence on AI as their top concern. Job displacement ranks lower, at 34%.


Lark (commissioned research)


900 employers and over 5,000 employees across six Southeast Asian markets


72% believe AI could eventually make their roles obsolete.


ADP People at Work 2026


Over 13,000 respondents across Asia-Pacific


Only 15% of Singapore employees feel confident about their job security.


Read the first and you'd conclude employees are optimistic and mainly worried about losing their edge. Read the second and you'd conclude most expect to be replaced. Read the third and you'd conclude Singapore is anxious about everything.


There's a fourth signal too. On the WiN World AI Index, Malaysia's overall AI score rose from 60.5 to 67.4 this year, but its comfort score fell from 42.5 to 38.7. People are using AI more and liking it less.


## Why the data conflicts


**The questions are different.** Asking people to rank their top concern produces a very different answer from asking whether AI "could eventually" make their role obsolete. "Eventually" is an easy word to agree with.


**The sponsors are different.** Lark sells an AI workspace. ADP sells payroll and HR services. Milieu is a research firm. Nobody here is being dishonest, but every survey reflects what its sponsor wants to understand. (Yes, inFeedo sells something too. That's exactly why we're telling you to ask your own people.)


**The reality is different from company to company.** A 2026 Ministry of Manpower survey in Singapore found that 71.5% of firms had not begun adopting AI, while only 3.8% had fully integrated it into core processes. An employee at a company that hasn't started will answer very differently from one at a company restructuring around it.


**The headlines are moving.** The ILO found that employment in the occupations most exposed to AI has kept growing across Southeast Asia. Yet some well-known regional employers have announced AI-related job cuts. Employees read both stories.


## What the surveys agree on


Strip out the framing and three findings show up again and again.


**People don't know where AI ends and their job begins.** Lark's research describes a growing trust gap, with 79% of employees calling AI adoption at their workplace uneven and unsystematic.


**Data security worries them.** Data security and privacy rank as the top barrier to AI adoption in most markets Milieu studied, cited by 50% of respondents in Singapore.


**Training is uneven.** Lark warns of a two-tier workforce forming between employees who are being trained to use AI and those being left behind.


The common thread isn't fear of AI. It's fear of not being told what AI means for them.


## How to find out what your people actually think


**1. Ask before you roll out, not after.** Measure change readiness before launch, so you have a baseline to track against.


**2. Ask specific questions.** "Do you fear AI?" gets you a headline. "Which parts of your work do you expect AI to change, and what support would help?" gets you a plan.


**3. Ask again at the moments that matter.** The announcement, the first training, 30 days after go-live, 90 days after. Sentiment shifts quickly once people actually use the tools.


**4. Make it safe to be honest.** Few people will admit to their manager that they're worried about becoming obsolete. Anonymous or clearly confidential channels get the real answer.


**5. Segment the results.** By country, function and seniority. If a two-tier workforce is forming, you'll only see it in the cuts, not the average.


**6. Tell people what you heard and what happens next.** Which roles will change, which won't, and what training is coming. Silence is what turns uncertainty into anxiety.


## The bottom line


Regional AI surveys are useful for context and useless as a substitute for listening. Your employees' view of AI depends on your company's choices: how fast you move, what you tell them, and whether you train everyone or only some. The only reliable data on that is your own.
